title: Can you change the scope (access modifier) of an overridden method, and what are the rules (widen only; private/static/final restrictions)?
shortTitle: Can you change the access scope of an overridden method?
keyPoints: Yes, you can change the access modifier when overriding, but only to widen it (make more accessible)
Access order from narrow to wide: private, default (package-private), protected, public
You can move right (widen) but never left (narrow) when overriding
If parent method is public, child must keep it public because public is the widest modifier
Private methods are not inherited and therefore cannot be overridden
Static methods are hidden (compile-time binding), not overridden (no dynamic dispatch)

s1_definition.oneliner: Widen OK (protected to public). Narrow NOT OK (public to private). Private is not inherited. Static is hidden. Final is sealed. The Liskov Substitution Principle requires the child to be at least as accessible as the parent.
s1_definition.profdef:
Yes, you can change the access modifier when overriding, but only to widen it (make more accessible).

- **Access modifier order** (narrow to wide): `private` -> `default` (package-private) -> `protected` -> `public`.
- **Widening is valid**: `protected` in parent can become `public` in child.
- **Narrowing is invalid**: `public` in parent cannot become `private` or `protected` in child.
- **Private methods** are not inherited. The child does not see them. If the child defines a same-name method, it is a new method, not an override.
- **Static methods** are class-level. They bind at compile time to the variable type. A child can define a same-name static method, but this is method hiding, not overriding.
- **Final methods** are sealed. The compiler prevents any child from overriding them.
s1_definition.analogy: Head office at National Bank of India publishes a procedure visible to all branches (protected). Mumbai branch can make it visible to everyone (public): more people can see it, which is fine. But Mumbai branch cannot make it visible to only the branch manager (private): that would break branches that already follow the procedure. If head office marks a procedure final, no branch can modify it. If head office keeps a procedure private, branches do not even know it exists.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ACCESS MODIFIER HIERARCHY
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  private  ->  default  ->  protected  ->  public
  (most                                   (least
   restrictive)                            restrictive)

  Override rule:
  ──────────────────────────────────────→
  CAN widen (move right)
  ←──────────────────────────────────────
  CANNOT narrow (move left)

  CANNOT OVERRIDE:
  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │ private   │  │ static   │  │ final    │
  │ not       │  │ hidden   │  │ sealed   │
  │ inherited │  │ compile  │  │ no       │
  │           │  │ time     │  │ override │
  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, you can change the access modifier when overriding, but only to widen it. The order from narrow to wide: private, default, protected, public. You can move right (widen) but never left (narrow). If the parent method is protected, the child can make it protected (same) or public (wider), but not default or private (narrower). If the parent method is public, the child must keep it public because public is already the widest. This rule exists because of the Liskov Substitution Principle: code written against the parent expects a certain accessibility level, and the child must maintain at least that level.

Three types of methods cannot be overridden. Private methods are not inherited: the child does not even know they exist. Static methods are class-level: they bind at compile time to the variable type, not the object type. A child can define a same-name static method, but this is method hiding, not overriding. Final methods are explicitly sealed: the compiler prevents any child from changing their behavior.

Remember one sentence: you can widen access when overriding (protected to public) but never narrow it, and private, static, and final methods cannot be overridden at all.
